1. Abstract This report describes an end-to-end deep learning pipeline for music genre classification on the Messy Mashup Kaggle competition. The core challenge is a significant distribution mismatch: the training data consists of clean instrument stems, whereas the test set comprises noisy cross-song mashups. The solution addresses this through on-the-fly mashup simulation during training, ESC- 50 environmental noise augmentation at controlled signal-to-noise ratios, and class-weighted loss functions. Three distinct model families were developed and compared: a classical ML baseline using MFCC features with LightGBM, a custom-built AttentionCRNN (CNN + Bidirectional GRU + attention pooling), and two fine-tuned pretrained audio transformers (Wav2Vec2-base and the Audio Spectrogram Transformer pretrained on AudioSet). The AST model achieved a validation Macro F1 of 0.8828, with a weighted three-model ensemble further improving robustness. Test- Time Augmentation with five random crops per file was applied at inference. 

2. Introduction 2.1 Problem Statement The Messy Mashup competition requires classifying audio files into one of ten music genres: Blues, Classical, Country, Disco, Hip-Hop, Jazz, Metal, Pop, Reggae, and Rock. The training dataset provides 1,000 songs (100 per genre), each separated into four instrument stems: bass.wav, drums.wav, other.wav, and vocals.wav. Test samples are 3,020 noisy mashups created by mixing stems from different songs of the same genre, with random ESC-50 noise injected at varying intensities and positions. Evaluation uses Macro F1 Score, which treats all ten genres equally regardless of sample count. The primary difficulty is not the classification itself but the distribution gap: training and test data look fundamentally different. A model trained on clean stems will encounter very different spectral statistics at inference time. Bridging this gap is the central engineering challenge of this project. 2.2 Project Objectives • Develop at least three architecturally distinct models satisfying L1 viva requirements • Bridge the train/test distribution gap through realistic data augmentation • Achieve Macro F1 >= 0.80 on the Kaggle public leaderboard 

• Track all experiments with Weights and Biases for reproducibility • Maintain modular, well-documented code in GitHub across all milestones

This gives 4,000 individual audio files for training, each approximately 30 seconds long at 44.1kHz stereo. The ESC-50 auxiliary dataset provides 2,000 environmental sound clips across 50 classes, used for noise augmentation. The test set contains 3,020 unlabeled mashup files. 3.2 Exploratory Data Analysis An initial EDA pass (Milestone 1) examined the dataset structure, file integrity, and audio properties. Key findings: • All 10 genres contain exactly 100 songs each, making the dataset balanced at the song level • Some songs contain silent or near-silent stems, particularly vocal tracks in instrumental genres. Files smaller than 4KB were flagged as corrupt and excluded, removing a small fraction of training data • Sample rate analysis confirmed all files are at 44.1kHz; no resampling anomalies were found in the source data • Silence analysis using librosa's effects.split with top_db=20 identified numerous vocal stems with silent segments exceeding 5 seconds, particularly in Jazz and Classical genres • The validation split was fixed at 17% using a seeded random shuffle, preserving genre stratification. This yielded 830 training songs and 170 validation songs 3.3 Data Preprocessing and Augmentation The key insight driving the augmentation strategy is that the test mashups are constructed by: (1) selecting one stem each from four different songs of the same genre, (2) summing them together, and (3) adding ESC-50 noise at a random position. Training samples were generated to mirror this process exactly: • Cross-song stem mixing: for each training sample, stems from four distinct songs of the same genre were loaded and summed. The drum track came from one song, vocals from a second, bass from a third, and other instruments from a fourth 

• SNR-controlled noise injection: ESC-50 clips were added to 60% of training samples at signal-to-noise ratios uniformly sampled from 8-20 dB. The SNR floor was chosen carefully as values below 8 dB caused models to learn noise patterns rather than genre cues, leading to collapse on disco and rock classes • Rock/country confusion fix: confusion matrices consistently showed 50%+ of rock samples misclassified as country. 4. Audio Feature Representation Unlike text NLP tasks, audio requires converting raw waveforms into model-appropriate representations. Three distinct strategies were used across the three model families: 4.1 MFCC Feature Vectors (Classical ML) For the Milestone 2 classical ML baseline, each audio clip was converted into a 150-dimensional feature vector per stem, yielding a 750-dimensional concatenated feature vector per song (4 stems + mix). Features included 40 MFCC coefficients (mean and std), delta MFCCs, 12 chroma features (mean and std), mel spectrogram statistics, spectral centroid, rolloff, bandwidth, contrast, zero crossing rate, RMS energy, and tempo. StandardScaler normalization was applied before fitting. 4.2 Mel-Spectrograms (CNN and CRNN) For the CNN (Milestone 3) and CRNN (Milestone 4) models, raw waveforms were converted on- the-fly to dB-scaled mel-spectrograms using torchaudio. Parameters used: n_fft=1024, hop_length=256, n_mels=128, f_min=20 Hz, f_max=8000 Hz (half of 16kHz SR). Each mel- spectrogram was per-sample normalized to zero mean and unit variance. SpecAugment was applied during training: frequency masking with param=24 and time masking with param=80. 4.3 Raw Waveforms (Wav2Vec2 and AST) Wav2Vec2 operates directly on raw 16kHz waveforms via its internal 7-layer CNN feature extractor, requiring no hand-crafted preprocessing. The AST model uses its own internal feature extractor (AutoFeatureExtractor) which converts 16kHz waveforms to a fixed mel-spectrogram format with 128 mel bins and a sequence length of 1024 time steps, designed specifically for AudioSet-compatible input.

Architecture: AST adapts the Vision Transformer (ViT) for audio by treating a mel-spectrogram as a 2D image. The spectrogram is divided into 16x16 patch embeddings with positional encoding, and a standard 12-block transformer encoder processes the patch sequence. The CLS token is used for classification in the original model. Our fine-tuning replaced the classification head with a custom two-layer head (FC(256) -> GELU -> Dropout(0.3) -> FC(10)) and pooled over the full patch sequence excluding CLS, finding this more stable for a 10-class task. Fine-tuning strategy: the patch embedding layer and the first eight of twelve transformer blocks were frozen. Only the last four blocks and the classification head were trained, totaling approximately 28.5 million trainable parameters. AdamW optimizer with learning rate 3e-5 and weight decay 0.01 was used. ReduceLROnPlateau scheduler with patience=3 and factor=0.5 was chosen over cosine annealing after observing that hard LR resets caused large validation performance crashes. Training ran for up to 20 epochs with early stopping at patience=8. The AudioSet pretraining is the key advantage of this model: the network has already learned to distinguish music genres, instrument timbres, and environmental sounds before any fine-tuning, making it highly sample-efficient on our 830-song training set. 5.2 Model 2: AttentionCRNN (Built from Scratch) The AttentionCRNN is a fully custom architecture designed to capture both local spectral patterns and global temporal structure in audio, making it appropriate for distinguishing music genres where rhythm, instrumentation, and musical phrasing all contribute to genre identity. Architecture: the model receives a raw 16kHz waveform and internally converts it to a 128-bin mel-spectrogram. This is processed through four CNN blocks, each containing a 3x3 convolution, BatchNorm, and ReLU. Blocks 1-3 include MaxPool(2) while Block 4 uses AdaptiveAvgPool to fix the frequency dimension to 8 regardless of input length. The resulting (B, 128, 8, T') tensor is reshaped to (B, T', 1024) and passed through a 2-layer bidirectional GRU with hidden size 128, producing (B, T', 256). An attention mechanism computes a weighted sum over T' time steps using a learned linear layer, producing a single (B, 256) context vector. A final classifier FC(128) -> ReLU -> Dropout(0.4) -> FC(10) produces genre logits. During training, SpecAugment was applied to the mel-spectrogram before the CNN: frequency masking with param=24 and time masking with param=80. The attention pooling was a deliberate design choice over max pooling, as genre classification often depends on characteristic passages that may appear at any temporal position; attention allows the model to locate and upweight these passages automatically. 5.3 Model 3: Fine-Tuned Transformer —

representations before any fine-tuning, and needed only to adapt its final few transformer blocks to our specific 10-class task. Wav2Vec2 underperformed expectations relative to AST for a structural reason: it was pretrained on speech (LibriSpeech), not music. While its temporal modeling is strong, its features are less aligned with musical genre cues. The gap illustrates the importance of domain-appropriate pretraining rather than just model scale. Per-class error analysis revealed rock and country as the most confused pair throughout the project. Both genres share acoustic guitar timbre and similar tempo ranges. The targeted rock/country confusion fix (swapping other.wav stems during training) reduced this confusion but did not eliminate it, suggesting that the overlapping musical features are genuinely difficult to separate from 10-second clips. Test-Time Augmentation contributed a consistent improvement by averaging softmax probabilities over five random crops of each test file. This is particularly valuable for longer mashups where genre cues may be concentrated in specific segments. 6.4 Training Stability Observations A key finding from repeated experiments was that aggressive noise augmentation (NOISE_PROB=0.85, SNR_MIN=3 dB) caused catastrophic forgetting in disco and rock classification. After reducing to NOISE_PROB=0.60 and SNR_MIN=8 dB, models maintained consistent performance on these difficult genres. Similarly, unfreezing too many transformer layers (9 of 12 in Wav2Vec2) caused instability on the relatively small 830-song training set. The CosineAnnealingWarmRestarts scheduler caused periodic validation crashes; switching to ReduceLROnPlateau with patience=3 eliminated these spikes. 

7. Conclusion and Future Work 7.1 Key Learnings The most significant learning from this project is that the choice of training data distribution matters more than model architecture. Early experiments with clean-stem training produced Macro F1 around 0.55 regardless of model complexity. The cross-song mashup simulation increased this to 0.74 with a modest CRNN and to 0.88 with a pretrained AST. Domain-appropriate pretraining (AudioSet vs LibriSpeech) also proved critical: both Wav2Vec2 and AST are large transformer models, but their performance differed by nearly 20 F1 points due to the pretraining domain mismatch.
